9. Build the Difference column. In the first Difference cell, enter a formula that subtracts Planned from Actual, for example =C2-B2. Press Enter, then use the fill handle, the small square at the bottom-right corner of the selected cell, to drag the formula down the column. Every row now shows whether you spent more or less than planned.

10. Format for readability. Select your number columns and apply a currency format from the toolbar. Use bold text and a fill color for section headers and totals so the structure is easy to scan.

Practical tips: Always start formulas with an equals sign, or the spreadsheet treats your entry as text. Use cell references rather than retyping numbers inside formulas, so updates flow through automatically. If a formula shows an error, check for empty cells or text where a number should be. Save a copy of your budget as a template so you can reuse it each month without rebuilding the formulas. Finally, keep the layout simple: a clean grid of categories, planned amounts, actual amounts, and differences is easier to maintain than an elaborate design, and it will serve you well month after month.

title: software quick-start guide|creating a spreadsheet budget with formulas
text:
Set up your columns before you type a single number. In cell A1 put "Item," B1 "Category," C1 "Planned," D1 "Actual," E1 "Difference." Widen column A by dragging the divider between the A and B headers until the longest label fits; nothing kills a budget faster than a wall of . Save the file now, before you've entered anything, and save again every few minutes. You know how this ends otherwise.

Rows 2 through 6 are your fixed costs: rent or mortgage, utilities, phone, insurance, loan payments. Leave row 7 blank as a visual break. Rows 8 through 14 are variable spending: groceries, gas, dining out, subscriptions. Row 15 blank. Row 16 is where the math starts.

In E2, type =D2-C2 and press Enter. That gives you the variance for the first line. Click E2, grab the small square in the bottom-right corner of the cell, and drag down through E6. Then do the same for E8 through E14. If you'd rather not drag, select E2:E6, press Ctrl+D (Cmd+D on a Mac), and the formula fills down. Note the direction: Actual minus Planned. A positive number means you overspent, which is the opposite of how some templates do it. Pick a convention and stick to it, or you'll misread your own sheet in a month.

Totals go in row 17. In C17: =SUM(C2:C6)+SUM(C8:C14). Don't just select C2:C14, because that would sweep in the two blank spacer rows—harmless with SUM, but sloppy, and sloppy formulas have a way of becoming wrong formulas later. Copy that formula across to D17 and E17. For E17 you can also use =D17-C17; same answer, fewer things to break.

Here's the part most quick-starts skip. Percentages. In F1 type "% Used." In F2: =D2/C2, formatted as a percentage. If C2 is zero you'll get a DIV/0! error, so wrap it: =IF(C2=0,"",D2/C2). Fill that down the same way you filled the differences. Now a glance tells you the electric bill ran 112% of plan while the phone bill sat at 94%. That's the whole point of the column.

One more formula worth the thirty seconds: conditional formatting on the Difference column. Select E2:E14, open Conditional Formatting, and add a rule that turns cells red when the value is greater than zero. Overspending now announces itself. You can add a second rule for green when the value is less than zero, though I'd argue the red is the one that earns its keep.

Enter your numbers in C and D only. Never type over a formula cell—if you do, the cell goes quiet and stops updating, and you won't notice until the totals are wrong. If you must change a formula, change it in the first row of its range and refill the column so every row stays consistent.

Name the sheet. Double-click the tab at the bottom, type something like "March," and press Enter. Right-click the tab and choose Move or Copy, tick "Create a copy," and you've got next month's skeleton with all the formulas intact and the numbers cleared—well, mostly cleared; delete the values in C and D yourself before you start.

title: fitness guide for beginners|a 20-minute bodyweight workout with warm-up
text:
A Beginner's Guide to a 20-Minute Bodyweight Workout

Starting a fitness journey can feel overwhelming, but you do not need expensive equipment or a gym membership to get moving. Your own body weight is a powerful and accessible tool. This guide outlines a simple, effective 20-minute bodyweight workout designed specifically for beginners. It includes a warm-up, a circuit of basic exercises, and a cool-down, all of which can be done in the comfort of your home.

Before you begin any workout, it is crucial to warm up. A proper warm-up increases blood flow to your muscles, improves flexibility, and significantly reduces the risk of injury. For this routine, dedicate five minutes to a dynamic warm-up. Start with one minute of marching in place, lifting your knees high. Then, perform 30 seconds of arm circles forward and 30 seconds backward to loosen your shoulders. Follow this with 30 seconds of gentle torso twists and 30 seconds of leg swings for each leg. Finish your warm-up with one minute of jogging in place at a light, comfortable pace. You should feel your body temperature rise and your joints begin to feel more mobile.

The main workout is a 15-minute circuit. You will perform five exercises for 45 seconds each, followed by 15 seconds of rest. After completing all five exercises, you have finished one round. Aim to complete three full rounds. This structure is designed to build strength and stamina without overwhelming you.

The first exercise is the Squat. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Keep your chest up and your back straight as you bend your knees and hips, lowering your body as if you are sitting in a chair. Go as low as you can comfortably, then push through your heels to return to the starting position. This exercise strengthens your legs and glutes.

The second exercise is the Modified Push-Up. Begin on your hands and knees, with your hands slightly wider than your shoulders. Keep your body in a straight line from your head to your knees. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, then push back up. This variation reduces the load on your wrists and upper body, making it perfect for beginners.

The third exercise is the Glute Bridge. Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Place your arms at your sides. Squeeze your glutes and lift your hips toward the ceiling until your body forms a straight line from your shoulders to your knees. Hold for a moment, then slowly lower your hips back down. This is excellent for strengthening your glutes and lower back.

The fourth exercise is the Bird-Dog. Start on your hands and knees with a neutral spine. Simultaneously extend your right arm forward and your left leg backward, keeping your hips and shoulders square to the floor. Hold for a second, then return to the starting position and switch to the opposite arm and leg. This exercise improves core stability and balance.

The final exercise in the circuit is the Standing March. Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart. Lift one knee up toward your chest, then lower it and repeat with the other leg, swinging your arms naturally as if you were marching. This keeps your heart rate up and improves coordination.

After completing your three rounds, it is time to cool down. Spend five minutes performing static stretches. Focus on the muscles you just worked: your quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, chest, and back. Hold each stretch for 20 to 30 seconds without bouncing. Remember to breathe deeply and listen to your body. Consistency is more important than intensity, so celebrate every step you take on your fitness journey.

title: family cookbook|chocolate chip cookies that stay soft, with ingredients and steps
text:
Soft and Chewy Chocolate Chip Cookies

Every family cookbook needs a chocolate chip cookie recipe, but this one earns its place because it solves the oldest complaint in baking: cookies that turn crisp by the second day. These stay soft for nearly a week in a sealed container, and the secret is not luck. It comes down to a few deliberate choices, and once you understand them, you can make these cookies soft every single time.

The first secret is brown sugar. This recipe uses more brown sugar than white because brown sugar holds moisture, thanks to the molasses in it. The second secret is melted butter rather than softened butter. Melted butter produces a chewier, softer crumb, while creamed butter tends to give you a cakier or crisper result. The third secret is a brief chill of the dough and a slightly underbaked cookie. Pull them from the oven when the centers still look a little glossy, and let them finish setting on the hot pan. That is where the softness lives.

Ingredients

2 and one quarter cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, melted and slightly cooled
1 cup packed light brown sugar
Half cup granulated sugar
2 large eggs, room temperature
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 cups semisweet chocolate chips

Steps

1. Whisk the flour, baking soda, and salt together in a medium bowl and set aside.

2. In a large bowl, stir the melted butter with both sugars until smooth and no lumps remain. Let it sit for a minute or two; the mixture will look shiny.

3. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla, until the mixture is glossy and slightly thickened.

4. Add the dry ingredients all at once and fold with a spatula until just combined. Stop the moment you no longer see streaks of flour. Overmixing develops gluten, which makes cookies tough.

5. Fold in the chocolate chips.

6. Chill the dough in the refrigerator for 30 minutes. This brief rest firms the butter so the cookies spread less and stay thick and soft. If you are short on time, 15 minutes is better than nothing.

7. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit and line two baking sheets with parchment paper.

8. Scoop the dough into balls about 2 tablespoons each and place them 2 inches apart on the sheets. For bakery-style cookies, press a few extra chocolate chips onto the tops.

9. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until the edges are just set and pale golden but the centers still look soft and slightly underdone. Do not wait for the centers to brown.

10. Let the cookies cool on the baking sheet for 5 minutes before moving them to a rack. This carryover heat finishes the centers gently.

Practical tips: store cooled cookies in an airtight container with a slice of sandwich bread; the bread gives up its moisture and keeps the cookies soft, and you simply replace the bread when it dries out. For longer storage, freeze baked cookies in a zip-top bag and thaw at room temperature. If your cookies turned out crisp anyway, the usual culprits are baking too long, using butter that was too warm, or skipping the chill. This dough also freezes beautifully: roll it into balls, freeze on a sheet, then bag them and bake from frozen, adding 2 to 3 minutes to the bake time. Make these for a bake sale, a lunchbox, or a rainy afternoon, and watch how quickly the plate empties.

title: air fryer cookbook|crispy salmon and roasted potatoes, with ingredients and steps
text:
CHAPTER 7: THE WEEKnight WINNER

Section: Crispy Salmon with Golden Roasted Potatoes

There is a moment in every home cook's life when the air fryer stops being a novelty and becomes a genuine lifeline. For me, it happened on a Tuesday in February, the kind of gray, drizzly evening when the last thing I wanted to do was babysit a skillet of splattering oil. I had two salmon fillets in the fridge, a bag of baby potatoes, and about thirty minutes before my daughter's bedtime routine began. I remember standing there, staring at the air fryer on the counter, and thinking: what's the worst that could happen? What happened was a revelation. The potatoes came out shatteringly crisp with fluffy centers, the salmon emerged with a crackly, golden crust while staying impossibly moist inside, and I had exactly one basket to wash. My daughter asked for seconds. My daughter never asks for seconds of salmon. That dinner has been in our weekly rotation ever since, and I suspect it will find a permanent spot in yours too.

The secret to this dish is a two-stage approach: the potatoes go in first because they need more time, and the salmon joins them for the final stretch. This staggered method means everything lands on the plate hot and perfectly cooked at the same moment. One important note before we begin: keep the salmon skin on. The skin is your built-in crispy shield, protecting the delicate flesh while turning golden and crackly on the outside. If your family doesn't eat the skin, that's fine, but cook with it on regardless.

Ingredients (serves 2)

For the potatoes:
- 1 pound baby potatoes, halved (quartered if large)
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1/2 teaspoon garlic powder
- 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/8 teaspoon black pepper

For the salmon:
- 2 salmon fillets (about 6 ounces each), skin on, patted very dry
- 1 teaspoon olive oil
- 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt
- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/2 teaspoon dried dill (or 1 teaspoon fresh, chopped)
- Lemon wedges, for serving

Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Preheat your air fryer to 400°F (200°C) for 3 minutes. Preheating is not optional here; it's the difference between roasted potatoes and steamed ones.

2. In a medium bowl, toss the halved potatoes with the olive oil, garlic powder, smoked paprika, salt, and pepper until evenly coated.

3. Add the potatoes to the air fryer basket in a single layer, cut sides down. Cook at 400°F for 12 minutes, shaking the basket halfway through. The cut faces should be browning nicely.

4. While the potatoes cook, prepare the salmon. Pat the fillets thoroughly dry with paper towels; moisture is the enemy of crispiness. Rub each fillet with olive oil, then season both sides with salt, pepper, and dill.

5. After the potatoes' 12 minutes are up, push them to one side of the basket. Place the salmon fillets skin-side down on the empty side, nestling them among but not on top of the potatoes.

6. Cook at 400°F for 8 to 10 minutes, depending on thickness. Start checking at 8 minutes. The salmon is done when it flakes easily with a fork and reaches 145°F at the thickest point. The skin should release easily from the basket.

7. Let the salmon rest for 2 minutes before serving. Plate alongside the potatoes and squeeze fresh lemon over everything.

Cook's Note: Every air fryer runs a little differently. If your potatoes are browning too fast, drop the temperature to 390°F. If your salmon is thicker than one inch, add 2 minutes. Trust your eyes and your thermometer, not just the clock.

title: vegetarian cookbook|chickpea and spinach curry, with ingredients and steps
text:
Chickpea and Spinach Curry

This is the curry I make when the cupboard is nearly bare and dinner still needs to happen. A tin of chickpeas, a bag of spinach, an onion, and a few warm spices come together into something far greater than the sum of its parts. The chickpeas give it substance, the spinach melts down to a silky green, and the tomato and spice base does the heavy lifting on flavour. It is mild enough for children, though you can dial up the heat with a chopped chilli or a pinch of cayenne. Serve it with rice, flatbreads, or both, and expect the pot to be scraped clean.

Serves four.

Ingredients

Two tablespoons of sunflower or rapeseed oil
One large onion, finely chopped
Three garlic cloves, crushed
A thumb-sized piece of fresh ginger, grated
One teaspoon of cumin seeds
One teaspoon of ground coriander
Half a teaspoon of ground turmeric
Half a teaspoon of garam masala, plus extra to finish
A quarter teaspoon of chilli powder, or to taste
One tablespoon of tomato purée
One 400 gram tin of chopped tomatoes
Two 400 gram tins of chickpeas, drained and rinsed
200 millilitres of vegetable stock or water
200 grams of spinach, washed if fresh
A squeeze of lemon juice
Salt and black pepper
A small handful of fresh coriander, chopped, to serve

Method

1. Warm the oil in a wide pan over a medium heat. Add the onion with a good pinch of salt and cook for eight to ten minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and golden at the edges.

2. Add the garlic and ginger and cook for one minute more, until fragrant. Do not let them brown or they will turn bitter.

3. Add the cumin seeds and stir for thirty seconds, then tip in the ground coriander, turmeric, garam masala, and chilli powder. Stir constantly for about a minute so the spices toast in the oil and lose their raw edge.

4. Stir in the tomato purée and cook for another minute, then pour in the chopped tomatoes. Bring to a gentle simmer and let it bubble for five minutes, until the sauce darkens slightly and thickens.

5. Add the chickpeas and stock, season with salt and pepper, and simmer uncovered for ten to fifteen minutes. The sauce should reduce and cling to the chickpeas rather than sit watery in the pan.

6. If using fresh spinach, add it in handfuls, stirring each batch until it wilts before adding the next. If using frozen spinach, thaw it first and squeeze out the excess water, then stir it through and heat for three to four minutes.

7. Finish with a squeeze of lemon juice and a final pinch of garam masala. Taste and adjust the salt, which curries almost always need more of than you expect.

8. Scatter with fresh coriander and serve.

Practical tips: Crush a few of the chickpeas against the side of the pan with the back of your spoon near the end of cooking; the starch they release thickens the sauce beautifully. If the curry looks dry before the spinach goes in, loosen it with a splash of water rather than more oil. Leftovers keep for three days in the fridge and taste even better the next day, as the spices settle. The curry also freezes well for up to two months; thaw overnight and reheat gently, adding a little water if needed. For a richer version, stir a tablespoon of coconut milk or yogurt through at the end, off the heat, so it does not split.

title: smartphone user guide for beginners|backing up photos and freeing storage
text:
Chapter 7: Backing Up Your Photos and Freeing Up Storage

Your smartphone's camera is wonderful, and that is exactly the problem. Every birthday, every sunset, every funny moment with the dog — click, click, click — and before you know it, your phone is warning you that storage is almost full. Photos and videos are usually the biggest space hogs on any phone, but the good news is that protecting them and freeing up space go hand in hand. This chapter shows you how, step by step.

First, understand what "backing up" means. A backup is simply a second copy of your photos stored somewhere other than your phone — in the cloud or on a computer. If your phone is lost, stolen, or damaged, your memories survive. Think of it as insurance for your photo album.

The easiest option for most beginners is cloud backup. If you have an iPhone, open Settings, tap your name at the top, then tap iCloud, then Photos. Turn on "Sync this iPhone." Every photo you take will now be copied to iCloud automatically whenever you are connected to Wi-Fi. Apple gives you 5 GB free; if your photo library is larger, you can pay a small monthly fee for more space. On Android phones, the equivalent service is Google Photos. Open the Google Photos app, tap your profile picture, and turn on "Backup." Google gives you 15 GB free, shared across its services — usually plenty for a year or two of casual photos.

Two golden rules apply to both systems. Rule one: back up over Wi-Fi, not mobile data, so you do not burn through your data plan. Rule two: plug your phone in while backing up for the first time, because a large photo library can take an hour or more and will drain your battery.

Once your photos are safely in the cloud, you can free up space on the phone itself. On iPhone, go to Settings, then General, then iPhone Storage. You will see a list of what is using space. Tap Photos and enable "Optimize iPhone Storage." This clever feature keeps small, compressed versions on your phone and stores the full-quality originals in iCloud — you will barely notice the difference when scrolling, but you may recover many gigabytes. On Android, open Google Photos, tap your profile picture, then "Free up space." This removes photos from your phone that are already safely backed up in the cloud. Do not worry — they remain visible in the Google Photos app and can be re-downloaded anytime.

If you prefer a physical backup, connect your phone to a computer with a USB cable. On iPhone, use the Photos app on a Mac or the Apple Devices app on Windows to import your pictures. On Android, simply open your phone's folder on the computer and copy the DCIM folder — that is where camera photos live — onto your hard drive. Do this once a month for extra peace of mind.

Finally, a few housekeeping habits. Delete blurry shots and duplicate screenshots as you go — they add up. Empty your "Recently Deleted" album every few weeks, because deleted photos stay there for thirty days and still occupy space. And check your backup once in a while: open your cloud app and confirm that today's photos appear there.

Backing up takes ten minutes to set up and then runs quietly in the background forever. Freeing storage takes even less. Do both this week, and your phone will thank you — with more room for the next thousand memories.
